title: Second life: We have packaged ourselves into madness
gist: Two sachets of Thai curry paste ordered through Amazon arrived buried in a reused 56-tin cat-food crate, prompting a comparison with Soviet 'coarse, grey-brown' wrapping paper — the one consumer good the USSR never ran short of, because it had so much elite privilege to conceal. The argument is that western over-packaging conceals an equivalent void: an I-don't-care attitude driving millions of tonnes of waste into the oceans, and a visible gap between Amazon's minimal-packaging pledge and its practice.

themes.theme: E-commerce packaging waste as observed practice

insights.claim: Two small sachets of Thai curry paste ordered through Amazon from the Coconut Kitchen arrived buried under rumpled brown paper in a reused crate labelled 'Untamed Cat Food. Contains 56 Tins' — a container the size of a small shipping container for a pocket-sized order.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Ground-level evidence that third-party marketplace fulfilment, not just first-party logistics, drives packaging excess — a reputational and regulatory exposure for marketplace operators as packaging rules tighten.
insights.quote: “Warning: if left empty and unattended this box will contain a cat”
insights.locator: It was a courier, holding—with both hands

insights.claim: Amazon routinely dispatches minuscule orders in brand new and disproportionately large cardboard or plastic envelopes, in contradiction to its own pledge to use as little packaging as possible.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: A stated sustainability commitment visibly contradicted at the customer touchpoint is the kind of gap that attracts extended-producer-responsibility enforcement and ESG scrutiny.
insights.quote: in contradiction to its pledge “to use as little packaging as possible”
insights.locator: At least the Coconut Kitchen, or whoever did the packaging

insights.claim: Reusing a giant cat-food crate, however absurd the result, is preferable to dispatching a tiny order in brand new oversized packaging — secondary use of existing containers is the mitigating behaviour worth noticing.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Distinguishes reuse from virgin-material excess — the metric that actually matters for packaging footprint is new material consumed, not parcel size.
insights.locator: At least the Coconut Kitchen, or whoever did the packaging

insights.claim: It is no longer unusual to receive a pocket-size paperback or a blister packet of pills in a plastic bag large enough to hold all seven volumes of Proust's In Search of Lost Time, inverting the old adage about good things coming in small packages.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Packaging-to-product ratio has deteriorated across online and retail channels, implying rising per-order material and freight-volume costs that will eventually be priced or regulated.
insights.quote: good things no longer come in small packages, but get delivered in enormous parcels
insights.locator: I cannot help noticing that Amazon and some other companies

insights.claim: An Amazon order for Guy Armstrong's book 'Emptiness. A Practical Guide for Meditators' arrived in an oversized brown envelope that was literally empty, and the replacement shipment meant two large pieces of cardboard went into the waste bin for one book delivered.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Fulfilment errors double the packaging footprint and the shipping cost per unit delivered — pick-accuracy is an underappreciated sustainability and margin lever in e-commerce.
insights.quote: inside the envelope was pure emptiness (or “sunyata”, in Sanskrit)
insights.locator: A couple of years ago, to satisfy my growing interest in Buddhism

themes.theme: Soviet packaging as a concealment technology

insights.claim: The German historian Karl Schlögel devoted pages of 'The Soviet Century: Archaeology of a Lost World' to the USSR's coarse grey-brown wrapping paper, noting that the same paper served for a loaf of bread or a newly bought ring and was representative of an entire period.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: A single undifferentiated packaging standard is the material signature of an economy with no consumer branding — the inverse of the differentiation-driven packaging inflation seen in the west.
insights.quote: the same greyish-brown paper could be used for a loaf of bread or for a newly bought ring intended as a gift.
insights.locator: In my first, Soviet, life, packaging was easy

insights.claim: Soviet grey-brown wrapping paper served an unremarked function that Schlögel omits: concealing the contents of 'zakazi', special food parcels for the elite collected from 'zakritiy magazin' closed stores in central Moscow from which ordinary people were barred.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Packaging can be an inequality-management technology, not just a logistics input — a lens for reading any distribution system where visible consumption is politically sensitive.
insights.locator: The respected professor didn’t mention, however

insights.claim: The parcels contained items permanently unavailable in ordinary Soviet shops — oranges, chocolates, slices of ham, at times a tin of caviar — and Red Army top brass retained entitlement to these special supplies even after their deaths, via their widows.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Illustrates how deeply parallel distribution systems become embedded and inheritable in shortage economies — a durable pattern in state-allocated goods regimes.
insights.locator: The thick wrapping paper was indispensable

insights.claim: Coarse grey-brown wrapping paper was the one consumer item the USSR never experienced shortages of, precisely because there was so much to conceal, and recycling of anything other than stale communist dogmas was not an issue.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Supply abundance in a shortage economy tracks political function rather than consumer demand — a useful heuristic when reading state-directed production priorities.
insights.quote: This “coarse grey-brown wrapping paper” was one consumer item of which the USSR experienced no shortages, for there was a lot to conceal.
insights.locator: This “coarse grey-brown wrapping paper” was one consumer item

insights.claim: Western superfluous packaging conceals a non-Buddhist spiritual emptiness — an all-permeating I-don't-care attitude — which is the mechanism by which millions of tonnes of plastic and other waste reach the oceans.
insights.speaker: Vitali Vitaliev
insights.so_what: Frames packaging waste as a demand-side indifference problem rather than a technology problem, implying regulation or price signals — not innovation — are the binding lever.
insights.quote: But here, in the west, what are we trying to hide under the hugely superfluous packaging?
insights.locator: But here, in the west, what are we trying to hide
